slides.title: PSGN: Red Flags You Must Not Miss
slides.subtitle: High-yield acute nephritic syndrome revision for NEET-PG & INI-CET

slides.title: Classic Presentation & Latent Period
points: Age: **5–12 years** (rare <3 yrs) with slight male predominance
Latent period: **1–2 weeks** post-pharyngitis; **3–6 weeks** post-pyoderma
Classic triad: **Cola-colored hematuria**, **edema**, and **hypertension**
Often accompanied by **oliguria** and sub-nephrotic proteinuria
slides.highlight: Exam pearl: Synpharyngitic hematuria (1–2 days) points to IgA nephropathy!

slides.title: Red Flags: Urgent Complications
points: **Hypertensive encephalopathy**: headache, vomiting, seizures, altered sensorium
**Acute pulmonary edema**: tachypnea, orthopnea, basal creps, gallop rhythm
**Acute kidney injury**: severe oliguria/anuria, rising creatinine, hyperkalemia
**Congestive heart failure**: tender hepatomegaly, raised JVP from fluid overload
slides.highlight: Red flag: Seizures or vision changes in PSGN = Hypertensive emergency!

slides.title: Must-Know Labs & Biopsy Findings
points: **Low C3** (normalises in **6–8 weeks**); serum **C4 is normal**
**ASO titre** rises post-pharyngitis; **Anti-DNase B** best post-pyoderma
Urine: **Dysmorphic RBCs** and **RBC casts** confirm glomerular origin
LM: **Diffuse endocapillary proliferation**; EM: **Subepithelial humps**
IF: **Starry-sky** granular deposits of **IgG and C3**
slides.highlight: Red flag: C3 low >8–12 weeks? Think MPGN or C3 glomerulopathy!

slides.title: PSGN vs IgA Nephropathy (PYQ)
slides.subtitle: PSGN || IgA Nephropathy
points: Latent: 1–6 weeks post-infection || Synpharyngitic (1–2 days)
Complement C3: Low (normal in 6–8 wks) || Normal C3 levels
IF: Starry-sky IgG & C3 deposits || Mesangial IgA deposits
Prognosis: >95% complete recovery || Can progress to CKD

slides.title: Red Flags: Indications for Biopsy
points: **Persistent low C3** lasting beyond **8–12 weeks**
**Persistent nephrotic proteinuria** or gross hematuria >4 weeks
**Rapidly progressive** renal failure (suspected RPGN/crescents)
Absent latent period or **systemic signs** (rash, arthralgia — SLE/HSP)
slides.highlight: Exam pearl: Routine renal biopsy is NOT needed in typical PSGN.

slides.title: Management & Emergency Doses
points: First-line: **Salt & fluid restriction** with strict I/O and BP charting
Edema / HTN: **IV Furosemide 1–2 mg/kg/dose** q6–12h (max 6 mg/kg/day)
HTN emergency: **IV Labetalol 0.4–1 mg/kg/hr** (max 3 mg/kg/hr)
Eradicate strep: **PO Amoxicillin 50 mg/kg/day** q12h × 10d (max 1 g/d)
slides.highlight: Red flag: In HTN emergency, reduce BP by ≤25% over the first 8 hours!

slides.title: High-Yield Exam Takeaways
points: **Group A Strep** (nephritogenic M types e.g. **12** throat, **49** skin)
**No role of steroids** in routine PSGN (reserved for crescentic RPGN)
**Antibiotics do NOT prevent** PSGN (unlike acute rheumatic fever)
slides.highlight: Exam pearl: Microscopic hematuria can persist up to 1–2 years benignly!
